content: 1. Reed et al. (2003) investigated the longitudinal changes in bone density associated with oral contraceptive use. Their findings were published in the journal Contraception. 2. Cobb et al. (2002) examined the relationship between oral contraceptive use and bone mineral density in white and black women as part of the CARDIA (Coronary Risk Development in Young Adults) study. Their results were published in Osteoporosis International. 3. Burr et al. (2000) demonstrated that both exercise and oral contraceptive use suppress the normal age-related increase in bone mass and strength at the femoral neck in women aged 18–31 years. This study was published in Bone. 4. Recker et al. (1992) explored bone gain in young adult women, with their findings published in JAMA. 5. Mazess and Barden (1991) analyzed the effects of age, dietary intake, physical activity, smoking, and birth control pills on bone density in premenopausal women. Their study appeared in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 6. Gambacciani et al. (2006) conducted a longitudinal evaluation of perimenopausal bone loss and assessed the effects of different low-dose oral contraceptive preparations on bone mineral density. Their findings were published in Maturitas. 7. Gambacciani et al. (1994) studied the effects of a low-dose oral contraceptive preparation on vertebral bone loss and metabolism in perimenopausal women. This research was published in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 8. Gambacciani et al. (1994) also investigated the impact of hormone replacement therapy using a low-dose oral contraceptive preparation on bone mineral density and metabolism in perimenopausal women. Their findings were published in Maturitas. 9. Gambacciani et al. (1999) evaluated the effects of a low-dose oral contraceptive preparation on bone quantitative ultrasound characteristics in perimenopausal women undergoing hormone replacement therapy. This study was published in Menopause. 10. Gambacciani et al. (2000) assessed the longitudinal effects of a low-dose oral contraceptive preparation on femoral bone loss and metabolism in perimenopausal women. Their findings were published in Osteoporosis International. 11. Volpe et al. (1997) examined the relationship between oral contraceptives and bone metabolism, with their findings published in the European Journal of Contraception and Reproductive Health Care. 12. Hansen et al. (1991) identified potential risk factors for the development of postmenopausal osteoporosis over a 12-year period. Their study was published in Osteoporosis International. 13. Shargil (1985) conducted a three-year prospective study on hormone replacement therapy using a triphasic contraceptive compound in perimenopausal women. The findings were published in the International Journal of Fertility. 14. Taechakraichana et al. (2000) performed a randomized trial comparing oral contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy on bone mineral density and coronary heart disease risk factors in postmenopausal women. Their results were published in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 15. Taechakraichana et al. (2001) investigated differences in bone acquisition among hormonally treated postmenopausal women with normal and low bone mass. Their findings were published in the Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand. 16. Bahamondes et al. (2013) studied the effects of hormonal contraceptives during breastfeeding on infant milk ingestion and growth. Their findings were published in Fertility and Sterility. 17. Espey et al. (2012) compared the effects of progestin-only pills and combined oral contraceptives on lactation in a randomized controlled trial. Their study was published in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 18. Kamal et al. (1970) investigated the clinical effects of steroids on the initiation of lactation. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 19. Kamal et al. (1969) examined the clinical effects of gestagens on lactation. Their study was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 20. Kapp and Curtis (2010) conducted a systematic review on the use of combined oral contraceptives among breastfeeding women. Their findings were published in Contraception. 21. Koetsawang et al. (1972) studied the effects of oral contraceptives on lactation. Their findings were published in Fertility and Sterility.
